nameStory: The snowy owl gets its name from its stunning white plumage, which makes it look like it's been dusted with fresh snow. This Arctic visitor is also called the polar owl or white owl, all names that celebrate its ghostly pale appearance that helps it blend into the snowy tundra where it breeds.
description: The snowy owl is a magnificent Arctic visitor that occasionally graces New England during winter months. This large, stocky owl is famous for its mostly white plumage, though females and young birds show beautiful dark brown markings scattered across their feathers. It's one of the biggest owls you'll see, with a distinctive round face and piercing yellow eyes. Unlike most owls, snowy owls are often active during the day, making them easier to spot than their nocturnal cousins.

idTips.label: White Plumage
idTips.description: Predominantly white feathers with varying amounts of dark brown barring - males are usually purer white while females show more extensive dark markings

idTips.label: Large Size
idTips.description: One of the largest owl species with a heavy, stocky build that's noticeably bigger than most other owls you'll encounter

idTips.label: Yellow Eyes
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow eyes that seem to glow, set in a rounded facial disc without the 'ear tufts' of great horned owls

idTips.label: Daytime Activity
idTips.description: Often seen hunting or perched in broad daylight, especially on fence posts, poles, or open ground - unusual behavior for most owls

idTips.label: Ground Perching
idTips.description: Frequently sits directly on the ground, snow, or low perches in wide-open spaces rather than hiding in dense trees

idTips.label: Feathered Feet
idTips.description: Heavily feathered legs and feet that look like fluffy white boots, an adaptation to their Arctic lifestyle

habitat: In New England, snowy owls appear in wide-open spaces that remind them of their Arctic tundra home. Look for them in coastal dunes, large agricultural fields, airports, salt marshes, and shoreline areas where they can scan for prey from elevated perches. They avoid dense forests, preferring expansive areas with good visibility where they can spot movement from great distances.

seasonality.spring: Most snowy owls begin their journey back north to Arctic breeding grounds, though some may linger into early spring. Look for them in the same open habitats before they disappear until next winter.
seasonality.summer: Extremely rare in New England during summer months as they're on Arctic tundra breeding grounds. Any summer sighting would be highly unusual and noteworthy.
seasonality.fall: The first arrivals from the north may appear in late fall, especially during years when Arctic prey is scarce. Young birds often arrive first, showing more dark markings.
seasonality.winter: Peak viewing season when these Arctic visitors are most commonly seen. Some years bring larger numbers than others, depending on food availability in their northern range.

funFact: Snowy owls are nomadic wanderers that rarely use the same nest site twice or even breed with the same mate in consecutive years - they're the ultimate free spirits of the owl world, following food sources across vast Arctic landscapes with no fixed address!
confusionNotes: In New England, snowy owls are most likely confused with barn owls, which are also pale-colored. However, barn owls have a heart-shaped white facial disc and peachy-buff coloring on their backs, while snowy owls are much larger, stockier, and have round faces with yellow eyes. Remember: barn owls have dark eyes and are strictly nocturnal, while snowy owls have bright yellow eyes and hunt during the day.
contextualKnowledge: Snowy owls are sometimes called 'Hedwig owls' after Harry Potter's famous pet, though the movies actually used trained barn owls and great horned owls painted white. Real snowy owls are wild Arctic birds that can't be kept as pets and need specialized care in captivity.
compareHints: Compared to their closest New England relative, the great horned owl, snowy owls are easily distinguished by their white plumage and lack of 'ear tufts' (the horn-like feather projections). Great horned owls are brown and heavily barred with prominent ear tufts, while snowy owls have smooth, rounded heads. Snowy owls are also much more likely to be seen during daylight hours in open areas, while great horned owls prefer wooded areas and are strictly nocturnal.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While the Snowy Owl is the only other species in the same genus found in New England, Great Horned Owls are easily distinguished by their prominent ear tufts, brown and gray mottled plumage, and year-round presence.
